column2: A SQL Server table can have at most {{c1::one}} PRIMARY KEY constraint.
column3:
One primary key can describe a pair such as (OrderID, LineNumber). You do not need a separate primary key for each column.
Review source

column2: Every column in a PRIMARY KEY must be {{c1::NOT NULL}}.
column3:
Every part must have a known value. A composite primary key rejects any candidate row with NULL in even one of its key columns.
Review source

column2: On a disk-based rowstore table, PRIMARY KEY {{c1::NONCLUSTERED}} creates a nonclustered supporting index.
column3:
The nonclustered index enforces the key separately from the table's storage order. The table can use a different clustered key.
Review source

column2: Define a parent reference with FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) {{c1::REFERENCES}} dbo.Customer(CustomerID).
column3:
REFERENCES names the parent table and key that the child value must match. The child column name does not need to be the same as the parent column name.
Review source

column2: If no referential action is specified for a SQL Server foreign key, the default is {{c1::NO ACTION}}.
column3:
Without an explicit action, SQL Server does not cascade a parent change to its children. It rejects a change that would break a reference.
Review source

column2: ON DELETE {{c1::SET DEFAULT}} assigns default values to the affected child foreign key columns.
column3:
SET DEFAULT changes the references while keeping the child rows. A non-NULL default still needs a matching parent key.
Review source

column2: A nullable column with a single-column UNIQUE constraint permits at most {{c1::one}} NULL value in SQL Server.
column3:
A single-column unique constraint treats a second NULL as a duplicate for uniqueness. A filtered unique index can enforce uniqueness only for non-NULL rows instead.
Review source

column2: SQL Server rejects the row when a CHECK predicate returns {{c1::FALSE}} rather than TRUE or UNKNOWN.
column3:
FALSE violates the rule. For example, CHECK (Price > 0) rejects zero, but a nullable Price evaluates to UNKNOWN and can still be stored as NULL.
Review source

column2: The column property that rejects SQL NULL values is {{c1::NOT NULL}}.
column3:
NULL means the value is missing. An empty string is a supplied character value, so reject it with a separate rule if necessary.
Review source

column2: For a nullable numeric Salary column, {{c1::CHECK (Salary >= 20000)}} rejects non-NULL salaries below 20000.
column3:
The predicate rejects a known value below 20000. It says nothing about whether a salary is required because a NULL comparison is UNKNOWN.
Review source

column2: Use the {{c1::DEFAULT}} keyword in VALUES to explicitly request a column's configured default value.
column3:
DEFAULT asks SQL Server for the configured value in that position. Explicit NULL supplies a value instead and does not request the default.
Review source

column2: Name a default in a column definition with IsActive BIT {{c1::CONSTRAINT}} DF_Activity_IsActive DEFAULT(1).
column3:
A named constraint lets deployment scripts refer to the same object name in every target. Without a name, SQL Server can assign a different generated name.
Review source

column2: For SQL Server BULK INSERT, specify {{c1::CHECK_CONSTRAINTS}} to validate CHECK and FOREIGN KEY constraints during the import.
column3:
This bulk-load option validates CHECK and foreign key rules on incoming rows. It is not needed to turn on uniqueness checks for primary and unique keys.
Review source

column2: Create a standalone number generator with {{c1::CREATE SEQUENCE}} dbo.OrderNumbers START WITH 1000 INCREMENT BY 1;
column3:
The sequence exists before or apart from any table that uses it. Request the next value with NEXT VALUE FOR or use that expression as a column default.
Review source

column2: Set a sequence's initial returned value with {{c1::START WITH}} 1000.
column3:
START WITH is the first value returned by the new sequence. It does not define the lower bound unless you set MINVALUE to the same number.
Review source

column2: Set a sequence's step size with {{c1::INCREMENT BY}} 5.
column3:
A positive step moves up and a negative step moves down. For example, a start of 100 and a step of 5 produce 100, 105, 110.
Review source

column2: Define a sequence's lower bound with {{c1::MINVALUE}} 1000.
column3:
The lower bound limits a descending sequence and is also where an ascending cycling sequence restarts. It need not equal START WITH.
Review source

column2: Define a sequence's upper bound with {{c1::MAXVALUE}} 999999.
column3:
For an ascending sequence, the next request fails or wraps when its increment would cross this bound. The configured cycling option determines which happens.
Review source

column2: To let a SQL Server sequence wrap to the opposite bound after reaching its limit, configure {{c1::CYCLE}}.
column3:
CYCLE returns to the opposite bound when the next step crosses a limit. It can reuse values, so it does not guarantee stored keys stay unique.
Review source

column2: New SQL Server sequences default to {{c1::NO CYCLE}} when no cycling option is specified.
column3:
With the default, the engine raises an error when the next value is out of bounds. Specify CYCLE explicitly if the application can safely accept reused numbers.
Review source

column2: To use dbo.OrderNumbers as a column default, write OrderNumber BIGINT DEFAULT ({{c1::NEXT VALUE FOR}} dbo.OrderNumbers).
column3:
When an insert requests the default, SQL Server takes a value from the named sequence. The sequence must be in the table's database.
Review source

column2: Set a sequence's next returned value to 1000 with ALTER SEQUENCE dbo.OrderNumbers {{c1::RESTART WITH}} 1000;
column3:
RESTART WITH changes what the sequence issues next. It does not update rows already stored, so a restart can cause duplicates if no constraint prevents them.
Review source

column2: Change an existing sequence's step to 5 with {{c1::ALTER SEQUENCE}} dbo.OrderNumbers INCREMENT BY 5;
column3:
ALTER SEQUENCE changes the generator without replacing it. The new increment controls later allocations, not the values already stored in rows.
Review source

column2: For sys.sp_sequence_get_range, declare the variable receiving @range_first_value OUTPUT as {{c1::SQL_VARIANT}}.
column3:
SQL_VARIANT lets the procedure return values from sequences with different underlying integer types. Convert the result explicitly if the caller needs a specific type.
Review source

column2: If AS data_type is omitted in CREATE SEQUENCE, the sequence's data type defaults to {{c1::BIGINT}}.
column3:
BIGINT is the default type of the sequence, not a requirement for every destination column. Choose the sequence type and its bounds to fit the consumer.
Review source
